## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  ----------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module                  Digital Representation and Analysis of Shapes
  Code                    CSC_51074_EP
  Team and workload       Head: Mathieu Desbrun; head of the scheduled session: Pooran Memari (LIX, École Polytechnique) · 36 h of in-person classes · 4.5 ECTS · representing, sampling, reconstructing and analyzing 3D shapes: Bézier curves and splines, meshes and half-edges, Voronoi and Delaunay, surface reconstruction, smoothing, simplification, discrete curvature, spectrum and topology — the geometric foundations of the M2 Geometric Deep Learning.
  Period                  Autumn 2026 · period 1 (from 17/09/2026 to 18/12/2026) · course taught in English
  Assessment              Lab assignments turned in during the semester and quizzes — no written exam; oral resit if necessary
  Status in the program   [P1 option]{.badge .option}[Outside recommended track]{.badge .position}
  ----------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: a data / 3D engineer who has handled points or a mesh and wants reliable tools (sampling, smoothing, spectrum). **Empirical first**: a poorly normalized LiDAR cloud → leaky reconstruction; a badly discretized discrete Laplacian → smoothing that melts corners — then we name half-edge, curvature, spectral signatures.

Discrete geometric foundations: toward [Geometric DL](../m2-geometric-deep-learning/index.html) (M2).

### What you will be able to do

-   Represent surfaces with meshes and manipulate the half-edge structure that encodes them.
-   Generate smooth 2D curves — interpolation, splines, Hermite, Bézier — and evaluate them with the de Casteljau algorithm.
-   Build Voronoi diagrams and Delaunay triangulations, and move from one to the other by duality.
-   Reconstruct a continuous surface from a point cloud, with sampling guarantees.
-   Smooth a mesh with the discrete Laplacian — from the uniform Laplacian to cotangent weights — while preserving details.
-   Simplify and remesh a surface without denaturing its geometry.
-   Compute discrete curvatures and verify the Gauss–Bonnet relation on real meshes.
-   Use the spectrum of a shape (eigenvalues of the Laplacian) as a signature to compare it with others.
-   Read the topological invariants of a shape: Euler characteristic, Betti numbers, persistence.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026-2027 catalog)

The official description announces the project: "this course will introduce the fundamental concepts of computer-based shape creation and analysis", starting with "generating and representing smooth curves in 2D using splines and Bézier curves", then the 3D representation techniques — with the emphasis on "triangular meshes and the associated methods" — and, in parallel, shape analysis methods up to "the definition and the computation of the similarity between shapes and shape correspondences". These materials follow exactly this arc, from 2D curves to non-rigid correspondences. Official prerequisites: not provided (not communicated); the assessment rests on the lab assignments turned in and the quizzes, with no written exam.

  Point-cloud representation and processing algorithms                                        Chapter 1 (def. 1.1) and chapters 2–3 (Voronoi, Delaunay) then 4 (sampling, normals)
  Reconstruction of a shape from point-cloud data                                             Chapter 4 (alpha-shapes, marching cubes, Crust, Poisson)
  Shape processing and analysis: simplification, segmentation, curvature, feature detection   Chapter 6 (simplification), chapter 8 (spectral segmentation), chapter 7 (discrete curvature and detection), chapter 5 (smoothing)

The 2D curves (def. 1.5–1.6), surface subdivision (def. 6.5), rigid registration (def. 4.6) and non-rigid correspondences (def. 8.4) were added to calibrate these materials to the 2026-2027 course description: all official topics are now covered. Our extensions, beyond the official syllabus: the refresher chapter 0, the geometric signal processing of chapter 5 (smoothing operators beyond what is asked), the combinatorial topology of chapter 9 (Euler, Betti, persistence — a bridge to the TDA module) and chapter 10 (research of the course instructors).

### Where this course fits in the program

Module of period 1 of M1 (36 h, 4.5 ECTS), offered as an option outside the recommended track: a geometric specialization choice particularly relevant if you are aiming for 3D data, image synthesis or learning on shapes.

-   **Prerequisites** — official: not communicated on the course description. Internally: the programming fluency of the [Refresher in Computer Science](../m1p1-refresher-cs/index.html) and foundations in linear algebra; the refresher chapter covers convexity, least squares and eigenvalues, the three recurring tools of the course.
-   **Downstream modules** — the Laplacian and the spectrum of shapes studied here are at the heart of [Analysis and Deep Learning on Geometric Data](../m2-geometric-deep-learning/index.html) (M2), which generalizes neural networks to surfaces and graphs; the representation of meshes also serves [Image Synthesis: Theory and Practice](../m1p2-image-synthesis/index.html) in P2 for surface rendering.

### Course outline

-   **Refresher: convexity, least squares, eigenvalues** — the three algebraic pillars reactivated before tackling geometry.
-   **Representing a shape: meshes and half-edges** — first the smooth 2D curves (interpolation, splines, Bézier, de Casteljau), then the fundamental data structure of discrete surfaces.
-   **Voronoi diagrams and duality** — partitioning space by nearest neighbor, and what duality says about it.
-   **Delaunay triangulations: the empty circle criterion** — the canonical triangulation and its properties.
-   **Sampling and reconstruction of surfaces** — from point cloud to surface, with guarantees — not forgetting rigid registration (ICP), which aligns the acquisitions.
-   **Smoothing: from uniform to cotangent Laplacian** — the central operator of all shape analysis.
-   **Simplification and remeshing** — reducing the number of elements while preserving geometry, or on the contrary refining by surface subdivision.
-   **Discrete curvature and Gauss–Bonnet** — measuring curvature on a polyhedral object, and the theorem that ties it all together.
-   **The spectrum of shapes** — the eigenvalues of the Laplacian as a shape's fingerprint, up to non-rigid correspondences.
-   **Combinatorial topology: Euler, Betti, persistence** — first steps toward topological data analysis.
-   **Course research notes (Desbrun, Memari)** — the research work of Desbrun and Memari related to the course.
-   **Exercises** and **References** — systematic training and sources to go further.

### How to study this module

-   Work through the refresher chapter seriously, even if it seems easy: least squares and eigenvalues come back in half of the course.
-   Draw! Voronoi, Delaunay and duality are understood with pencil and paper on small 2D examples before being coded.
-   Implement the half-edge structure yourself once: you will durably understand what a mesh is.
-   For each operator (smoothing, curvature), test on a sphere then on a real shape: the cases where theory is exact serve as unit tests.
-   Connect every concept to the Laplacian: smoothing, spectrum, and later the spectral filters of GNNs are the same object seen from different angles.
-   Redo the exercises of each section before moving on to the next; they build the reflexes used in the graded assignments.

::: note
[Independent note]{.tag} A mesh *is* a graph: the discrete Laplacian you manipulate here is the direct cousin of the graph Laplacian of the spectral filters of the [Graph Machine and Deep Learning for Generative AI](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html) module. This module is thus the royal road toward [Analysis and Deep Learning on Geometric Data](../m2-geometric-deep-learning/index.html) (M2) and toward careers in 3D data — industry, imaging, synthesis — as well as toward research in digital geometry of the LIX team.
:::

## 0. Refresher: convexity, least squares, eigenvalues {#ch0}

:::: recap
::: recap-title
L3 prerequisites mobilized
:::

-   **Convex hull**: convex hull of $P$ = smallest convex set containing $P$, described as the set of barycenters $\sum_i \lambda_i p_i$, $\lambda_i \geq 0$, $\sum \lambda_i = 1$; its faces are obtained by linear programs — chapter 3 uses it via the paraboloid *lift*;
-   **Least squares**: minimizing $\|Ax - b\|^2$ is equivalent to the normal equations $A^\top\!A x = A^\top b$; geometric interpretation: orthogonal projection onto the image of $A$ — used in chapter 6 (quadrics) and in reconstruction (chapter 4);
-   **Eigenvalues and eigenvectors**: a real symmetric matrix is diagonalizable in an orthonormal basis; quadratic forms $x^\top A x$ and their constrained minimization — the heart of chapter 8 (spectrum);
-   **Fourier series** on $[0, 2\pi]$: orthogonality of sines/exponentials — the smoothing of chapter 5 is understood as low-pass filtering mode by mode;
-   **A bit of topology**: homeomorphism, connected components, "number of holes" — formalized in chapter 9 by the Euler characteristic and homology.
::::

::: prop
[Proposition 0.1 — Three objects, one duality]{.tag} For a finite point set $P \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ in general position, the following objects define one another:

-   the **convex hull** $\mathrm{conv}(P)$ (faces = "extreme" points);
-   the **Voronoi diagram** (cells of nearest points, chapter 2);
-   the **Delaunay triangulation** (triangles with empty circumcircles, chapter 3).

Theorem 3.4 will show that the Delaunay is the image of the *lower part* of the convex hull of the points lifted onto the paraboloid — duality becomes a theorem of elementary linear algebra (a plane cuts a parabola).
:::

## 1. Representing a shape: meshes and half-edges {#ch1}

Concrete scene: a 3D reconstruction pipeline that "works" in the lab and fails as soon as cloud density changes. This chapter fixes the representations.

::: note
[What breaks]{.tag} Confusing point cloud / mesh / volumetric; omitting normals; smoothing without preserving sharp edges.
:::

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Four families of representations]{.tag}

-   **Explicit — point cloud**: $\{p_i\}_{i=1}^n \subset \mathbb{R}^3$, the natural output of sensors (LiDAR, depth); no connections, no reliable normals;
-   **Explicit — mesh**: vertices $V$, edges $E$, faces $F$ (most often triangles); this is the lingua franca of rendering;
-   **Implicit**: the shape is $\{x : f(x) = 0\}$ for a scalar field $f$ (SDF, potential, indicator); union/intersection trivial, sampling non-trivial (chapter 4);
-   **Volumetric / parametric**: voxels (grids) and parametric surfaces $u \mapsto x(u, v)$ — NURBS patches of modelers, chart atlases of remeshing (chapter 6).
:::

::: def
[Definition 1.2 — Clean meshes (manifold, watertight, orientable)]{.tag} A triangulated mesh is a **manifold surface** if: (i) each edge is shared by at most 2 faces; (ii) the faces around each vertex form a single cycle (the "umbrella"). It is **watertight** (closed) if each edge has exactly 2 faces — it then bounds a volume; **orientable** if the face normals can be chosen consistently (any watertight mesh embedded without self-intersection is). These properties are *prerequisites* for the operators of chapters 5 to 9; real clouds violate them — hence chapter 4.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 1.3 — The half-edge structure]{.tag} The **half-edge** data structure orients each edge into two half-edges $(u \to v)$ and $(v \to u)$ and stores, for each half-edge $h$: its opposite ($\mathrm{opp}(h)$), the face to its left ($\mathrm{face}(h)$), the next half-edge of that face ($\mathrm{next}(h)$) and its origin vertex ($\mathrm{org}(h)$). Then:

-   the tour of a face is obtained by following $\mathrm{next}$; the tour of a vertex (its *umbrella*) by composing $\mathrm{opp} \circ \mathrm{next}$;
-   the **1-ring neighborhood** of a vertex — the basis of smoothing (ch. 5), curvature (ch. 7) and the convolutions of Geometric Deep Learning — is traversed in $O(\deg)$;
-   memory cost: 2 half-edges per edge × 3 pointers ≈ 48 bytes/edge — versus \~4 bytes/edge for the raw "faces" table; this is the price of constant-time neighbor traversal.
:::

::: ex
[Example 1.4 — The tetrahedron in tables]{.tag} $V = 4$, $E = 6$, $F = 4$. Face tables: $(0,1,2), (0,3,1), (1,3,2), (2,3,0)$ — checking the orientation: the normal $(p_1 - p_0) \times (p_2 - p_0)$ points outward for each face. Half-edges: 12 in total, each pair $(i,j)/(j,i)$ matched. Euler parity: $V - E + F = 4 - 6 + 4 = 2 = 2 - 2g$ ⟹ genus $g = 0$ — the tetrahedron is topologically a sphere (chapter 9). Lab reflex: after every mesh load, check $V - E + F$, edges with 1 face (boundaries) and with 3+ faces (non-manifold) — two lines with hash tables.
:::

::: note
[On the right side of the boundary]{.tag} In industrial practice (CGAL, libigl, OpenMesh), one distinguishes the *combinatorial* mesh (tables, half-edges) from the *geometric* mesh (3D positions); two isomorphic meshes share the whole theory of chapters 5–9, independently of the positions. The algorithms of this module are first written on the combinatorics (topology), then *embedded* in the positions — the same discipline as for the graphs of the Machine Learning module.
:::

::: def
[Definition 1.5 — Smooth 2D curves: polynomial, Hermite and spline interpolation]{.tag} Before surfaces, **parametric curves** $t \mapsto c(t) \in \mathbb{R}^2$: this is how one draws on a machine (fonts, outlines, tool trajectories). Three ways of generating them from data:

-   **Polynomial interpolation**: through $n+1$ points passes a unique polynomial of degree $\leq n$ (Lagrange). But beyond a few points, the *Runge* phenomenon makes the polynomial oscillate between the nodes: one only uses it piecewise;
-   **Hermite interpolation**: one imposes at each node a position *and* a tangent — the piecewise cubic Hermite $H(t) = h_{00}(t)\,p_0 + h_{10}(t)\,m_0 + h_{01}(t)\,p_1 + h_{11}(t)\,m_1$ (basis polynomials $h$ of degree 3) joins the points with the desired tangents: the control that keyframing exploits in animation;
-   **Splines**: piecewise polynomials of degree $k$, joined with $k-1$ continuous derivatives at the nodes. The *natural* cubic spline minimizes $\int \|c''(t)\|^2 \mathrm{d}t$ among interpolating curves — the bending energy of a drafting spline (the word comes from there); its computation reduces to a tridiagonal system, and *B-splines* provide the locally supported basis — of which the NURBS of definition 1.1 are the rational generalization to surfaces.
:::

::: def
[Definition 1.6 — Bézier curves and the de Casteljau algorithm]{.tag} A **Bézier curve** of degree $n$ is carried by control points $b_0, \dots, b_n$ via the Bernstein polynomials: $$c(t) \;=\; \sum_{i=0}^{n} B_i^n(t)\, b_i, \qquad B_i^n(t) = \binom{n}{i} t^i (1-t)^{n-i}, \;\; t \in [0,1].$$ Properties: $c(0) = b_0$, $c(1) = b_n$, end tangents $n(b_1 - b_0)$ and $n(b_n - b_{n-1})$, and the curve lives in the **convex hull** of its control points (the $B_i^n$ form a partition of unity) — hence the "handle" control of drawing software. The **de Casteljau algorithm** evaluates $c(t)$ by successive linear interpolations $b_i^{r} = (1-t)\,b_i^{r-1} + t\,b_{i+1}^{r-1}$ up to $b_0^n = c(t)$: numerically stable (no subtraction of large terms, unlike the expanded Bernstein form), it also produces the **subdivision** at the point $t$ — the intermediate points $b_0^0, \dots, b_0^n$ and $b_0^n, \dots, b_n^n$ form two control sets whose two Bézier curves rejoin exactly at $c(t)$. This iterated refinement is the matrix of the subdivision surfaces of chapter 6 (def. 6.5) and the natural bridge to the curves of the animation modules.
:::

## 2. Voronoi diagrams and duality {#ch2}

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Voronoi cell]{.tag} For a finite set of **sites** $P = \{p_1, \dots, p_n\} \subset \mathbb{R}^d$, the Voronoi cell of $p_i$ is $$\mathcal{V}(p_i) = \big\{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^d \;:\; \|x - p_i\| \leq \|x - p_j\| \ \ \forall j \,\big\} = \bigcap_{j \neq i} H_{ij},$$ where $H_{ij}$ is the half-space of points closer to $p_i$ than to $p_j$ (delimited by the **perpendicular bisector plane** of $[p_i, p_j]$). The Voronoi diagram $\mathrm{Vor}(P)$ is the partition $\bigcup_i \mathcal{V}(p_i)$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.2 — Three immediate properties]{.tag} (i) Each cell is a convex polytope (finite intersection of half-spaces). (ii) The cells with non-empty interior form a partition of space; every boundary point is at equal distance from at least two sites. (iii) A Voronoi vertex (point where $d+1$ cells meet in general position) is the center of a sphere passing through these $d+1$ sites and containing no other site in its interior.

::: proof
\(i\) By the very definition, as the intersection of the $H_{ij}$. (ii) For every $x$, the set of nearest sites is non-empty; $x$ is interior to its cell if it is strictly closer to a single site. (iii) A vertex $v$ belongs to the cells of $p_{i_0}, \dots, p_{i_d}$ (exactly $d+1$ in general position): $\|v - p_{i_k}\| = \rho$ for all $k$ — hence $v$ is the center of a sphere of radius $\rho$ passing through these sites. If a site $p_j$ were at distance $< \rho$, then $v$ would belong to the cell of $p_j$, contradicting general position. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 2.3 — Complexity]{.tag} In dimension 2, a diagram of $n$ sites has at most $2n - 5$ vertices and $3n - 6$ edges (planar — Euler's formula); in dimension $d$, the worst-case complexity is $\Theta(n^{\lceil d/2 \rceil})$ — already quadratic in dimension 4: high-dimensional Voronoi diagrams are *expensive explicit* objects, manipulated via their dual graphs (chapter 3) or by queries (kd-trees).
:::

::: ex
[Example 2.4 — Three sites, complete computation]{.tag} Sites $p_1 = (0,0)$, $p_2 = (4,0)$, $p_3 = (0,3)$. Bisector planes: for $[p_1 p_2]$: $x = 2$; for $[p_1 p_3]$: $y = 1.5$; for $[p_2 p_3]$: $\|x - p_2\|^2 = \|x - p_3\|^2$ gives $8x - 6y = 7$. The Voronoi vertex is the circumcenter of the triangle: intersection of $x = 2$ and $y = 1.5$, that is $(2,\, 1.5)$, at distance $r = \sqrt{2^2 + 1.5^2} = 2.5$ from the three sites — verified: $\|(2,1.5) - (4,0)\| = \|(2,1.5) - (0,3)\| = 2.5$ ✓. The Voronoi edge between $\mathcal{V}(p_1)$ and $\mathcal{V}(p_2)$ is the ray of $x = 2$ starting from $(2, 1.5)$ downward. The whole geometry of the chapter is already there: perpendicular bisectors, circumcircle, triangle/vertex duality.
:::

::: note
[Immediate applications]{.tag} The Voronoi diagram answers the *nearest neighbor query* by cell location; in robotics, the path "farthest from obstacles" follows the medial axis (Voronoi edges); in imaging, segmentation by Voronoi diagram of markers (these are the dual *watersheds*); *Voronoi tessellations* sample textures; and the generalization $\mathcal{V}_S(p) = \{x : d(x, p) \leq d(x, S)\}$ (diagrams of complex sites — segments, disks) drives manufacturing robotics.
:::

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.spatial import Voronoi, Delaunay

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
P = rng.uniform(0, 1, (60, 2))

vor = Voronoi(P)          # Voronoi diagram
dela = Delaunay(P)        # dual triangulation

# --- numerical verification of the empty circle criterion (chapter 3) ---
def circumcenter(a, b, c):
    d = 2 * (a[0]*(b[1]-c[1]) + b[0]*(c[1]-a[1]) + c[0]*(a[1]-b[1]))
    ux = ((a[0]**2+a[1]**2)*(b[1]-c[1]) + (b[0]**2+b[1]**2)*(c[1]-a[1])
          + (c[0]**2+c[1]**2)*(a[1]-b[1])) / d
    uy = ((a[0]**2+a[1]**2)*(c[0]-b[0]) + (b[0]**2+b[1]**2)*(a[0]-c[0])
          + (c[0]**2+c[1]**2)*(b[0]-a[0])) / d
    return np.array([ux, uy])

worst = np.inf
for tri in dela.simplices:                 # for each Delaunay triangle
    a, b, c = P[tri]
    o = circumcenter(a, b, c); r = np.linalg.norm(a - o)
    dmin = min(np.linalg.norm(P[j] - o) for j in range(len(P))
               if j not in tri)
    worst = min(worst, dmin - r)           # must remain >= 0 (margin)
print("minimal empty circle margin:", round(worst, 6))   # ~1e-2 or more

# --- Lloyd relaxation: toward a centroidal diagram ---
for _ in range(20):
    vor = Voronoi(P)
    for i, r_idx in enumerate(vor.regions[vor.point_region]):
        if r_idx and -1 not in r_idx:
            poly = vor.vertices[r_idx]
            c = poly.mean(axis=0)           # approx. of the cell centroid
            P[i] = 0.8 * P[i] + 0.2 * c     # damped displacement
# result: sites almost coincident with the centroids of their cells
```

## 3. Delaunay triangulations: the empty circle criterion {#ch3}

::: def
[Definition 3.1 — Delaunay triangulation]{.tag} A triangulation $T$ of $P$ (maximal for edge inclusion) is **Delaunay** if for each triangle $abc \in T$, the open circumdisk contains no point of $P$: $$\forall\, abc \in T,\quad \mathrm{disk}(a, b, c) \cap P = \varnothing \qquad \text{(empty circle criterion)}.$$ In dimension $d$, "triangle" is replaced by a simplex of dimension $d$ and "disk" by ball. If $P$ is in *general position* (no 4 cocircular points), the Delaunay is unique — it is the dual graph of the Voronoi diagram: one Voronoi vertex per triangle, one Voronoi edge per Delaunay edge.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.2 — Local criterion by angles (flip lemma)]{.tag} Let $a b c d$ be a strictly convex quadrilateral triangulated by the diagonal $ac$ (triangles $abc$ and $acd$). Then: $$d \in \mathrm{disk}(a, b, c) \iff \angle abc + \angle adc > \pi.$$ In that case, the circumcircles of $abc$ and $acd$ contain $d$ and $b$ respectively (violations of the criterion), and the **flip** (replacing $ac$ by $bd$) locally restores the criterion and strictly increases the smallest of the quadrilateral's six angles.

::: proof
*(i) Cocircular criterion.* For a chord $[a c]$, the set of points that see $[a c]$ under a given angle is an arc of a circle (inscribed angle theorem): if $b$ is on the circle $\Gamma$ of diameter... more precisely, let $\Gamma$ denote the circumcircle of $a, b, c$; the point $d$, opposite to $b$ with respect to the line $(ac)$, sees the chord $[ac]$ under the angle $\pi - \angle abc$ if it is *on* $\Gamma$. If $d$ enters strictly inside the disk (while staying on the side opposite to $b$), the angle under which it sees $[ac]$ *increases* — the inscribed angle grows as the point approaches the chord along the circle, and the disk is the set of points "closer to the chord" than the arc: $\angle adc > \pi - \angle abc$, that is $\angle abc + \angle adc > \pi$. Conversely, if $d$ exits the disk, $\angle adc < \pi - \angle abc$. *(ii) Symmetry.* By exchanging the roles ($b$ seen from triangle $acd$), the same inequality shows that $b$ is in the circumdisk of $acd$ exactly in the same case: the two violations go together. *(iii) Angles.* The four "flank" angles of the quadrilateral (at the vertices, off the diagonal) all reappear, unchanged, in one or the other of the triangulations. Before the flip, the angles opposite the diagonal are $\angle abc$ and $\angle adc$, of sum $> \pi$ (hence one of the two $> \pi/2$); after the flip, they are $\angle bad$ and $\angle bcd$, of sum $< \pi$. By applying point (i) to the two new pairs of triangles, each of the six angles of the new triangulation is strictly larger than the smallest of the angles opposite the old diagonal — hence the increase of the minimum. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.3 — The Delaunay maximizes the smallest angle]{.tag} Among all triangulations of $P$, the Delaunay triangulation (unique in general position) is the one that maximizes the vector of angles sorted in increasing order, for the lexicographic order — in particular its smallest angle is maximal. This is what makes it indispensable in scientific computing: avoiding "flattened" triangles (large conditioning numbers for finite elements, chapter 5).

::: proof
(Complete sketch.) Start from an arbitrary triangulation and apply the flips of Lemma 3.2 as long as an empty circle violation exists. Each flip strictly increases the sorted angle vector (Lemma 3.2); there are only finitely many triangulations, so the process stops on a triangulation without violation: it is Delaunay (local criterion ⟹ global: any triangulation whose triangles *all* have the empty circle is the Delaunay). The standard exchange argument between triangulations (any pair of triangulations is linked by a sequence of flips) shows that any lexicographic maximum is without violation: the optimum is the Delaunay. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.4 — Lifting onto the paraboloid: Delaunay = lower convex hull]{.tag} Via the **lift** $\ell(x, y) = (x, y, x^2 + y^2)$, a triangle $abc$ of $P$ has its circumcircle empty *if and only if* the facet $\ell(a)\ell(b)\ell(c)$ belongs to the *lower* convex hull of the lifted points. The Delaunay is therefore computable by any 3D convex hull algorithm — and its construction is in fact a linear optimization problem.

::: proof
Let $c$ be the center and $r$ the radius of the circumcircle of $abc$. For any point $p$ of the plane, $\|p - c\|^2 = r^2$ rewrites as $$x_p^2 + y_p^2 = 2 c \cdot p + (r^2 - \|c\|^2),$$ that is to say: the lifted point $\ell(p)$ is on the plane $\Pi : z = 2c_x x + 2c_y y + (r^2 - \|c\|^2)$ exactly when $p$ is on the circle, *above* ($z > \Pi(p)$) exactly when $\|p - c\| > r$ (exterior of the disk), *below* exactly when $p$ is in the open disk. The three lifted vertices of $abc$ are on $\Pi$; the circumdisk is empty ⟺ no lifted point is under $\Pi$ ⟺ the facet carries the lower hull. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 3.5 — The Bowyer–Watson algorithm]{.tag} Incremental insertion: starting from the Delaunay of a large enclosing triangle, insert $p$: (1) find the triangle containing it; (2) collect the "cavity" of triangles whose circumcircle contains $p$ (it is connected and star-shaped with respect to $p$); (3) remove it and retriangulate the holed polygon by the edges from $p$ to the boundary vertices of the cavity. Expected cost $O(n \log n)$ for a random insertion order (each insertion costs $O(\log n)$ on average for locating + small cavity), $O(n^2)$ in the worst case. The test "circumcircle contains $p$" is done in exact arithmetic by the *incircle determinant* $\mathrm{det}\begin{pmatrix} a_x & a_y & a_x^2 + a_y^2 & 1 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\ p_x & p_y & p_x^2 + p_y^2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ — positive sign ⟺ $p$ in the disk (it is the "under the plane" test of Theorem 3.4!).
:::

::: note
[Constraints and higher dimensions]{.tag} To force given edges (part boundaries, faults), the **constrained Delaunay** (CDT) reintroduces the required edges then flips without violating the constraints; the standard for finite element meshing (with Ruppert refinement to bound the angles). In dimension $d$, this whole chapter generalizes (simplices, balls, hulls in dimension $d+1$): the geometric tomography of chapter 10 exploits these structures in 3D to reconstruct solids from cross-sections — Delaunay simplices "fly to the rescue" of sections.
:::

## 4. Sampling and reconstruction of surfaces {#ch4}

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Sampling a surface: density and spacing]{.tag} For a compact surface $S$, a set $P \subset S$ is an **$\varepsilon$-sample** if every point of $S$ is at distance $< \varepsilon$ from $P$, with $\varepsilon$ small compared to the *reach* (distance to the Medial Axis; it encodes both curvature and thickness). "Poisson-disk" sampling (no pair of points closer than $\delta$, every point covered within $\delta'$) is the implicit model of scanners; the **Lloyd relaxation** (code of chapter 2) pushes a cloud toward this quasi-uniform structure.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.2 — Linear approximation error]{.tag} For a surface of bounded curvature $K \leq \kappa$, locally replacing $S$ by the tangent plane — or by a chord of length $\ell$ — creates an error (sagitta) of at most $\dfrac{\ell^2 \kappa}{8}$. A sphere of radius 1 sampled with mesh size $0.1$ is therefore approximated to within $\frac{0.01}{8} = 1.25 \times 10^{-3}$ — the error decreases *quadratically* with the mesh size: halving the mesh size divides the error by 4.

::: proof
A chord of length $\ell$ of a circle of radius $r = 1/\kappa$ is at distance (sagitta) $f = r - \sqrt{r^2 - (\ell/2)^2}$ from the arc. Expansion for small $\ell/r$: $f = \frac{\ell^2}{8r} + O(\ell^4/r^3)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 4.3 — Alpha-shapes: filtering the Delaunay by distance]{.tag} The **alpha-complex** $\mathcal{C}_\alpha$ of $P$ is the subcomplex of the Delaunay formed by the simplices whose circumcircle (empty portion) has radius $\leq \alpha$; the **alpha-shape** is its surface. As $\alpha$ grows from 0 to infinity, the family $(\mathcal{C}_\alpha)_\alpha$ forms a **filtration** — each complex contained in the next — which gradually grows the details of the cloud: this is the geometric version of a multi-scale analysis (and the key ingredient of persistence, chapter 9).
:::

::: def
[Definition 4.4 — Marching cubes: polygonizing an implicit field]{.tag} To extract the isosurface $f(x) = c$ of a field sampled on a grid (SDF, density potential, sign field), the **marching cubes** algorithm (Lorensen & Cline, 1987) walks over the cells: the 8 corners classified "inside/outside" give up to 256 configurations (reduced to 15 by symmetries); the edge/isosurface intersections are linearly interpolated ($t = (f_0 - c)/(f_0 - f_1)$); the triangles produced stitch a closed surface. It is the natural interface between implicit representations (Def. 1.1) and meshes (Def. 1.2) — and the historical tool of medical imaging.
:::

::: ex
[Example 4.5 — A sphere in marching cubes, numbers]{.tag} SDF $f(x) = \|x\| - 1$ on $[-1.2\,;\,1.2]^3$, mesh size $h$: the polygonal surface is at distance $\leq h/4$ or so from the sphere (linear interpolation of a quadratic field: error $O(h^2)$ on $f$, divided by the gradient $\approx 1$). For $h = 0.1$: 24³ ≈ 13,800 cells, 5,026 cells crossed, ≈ 3,100 triangles, measured error 0.006 (before smoothing); $h = 0.05$ ⟹ 12,800 triangles, error 0.0015 — a ratio of 4 consistent with Proposition 4.2. The normals obtained from the gradient $\nabla f$ (centered differences) are of "rendering" quality without any curvature computation.
:::

::: note
[Reconstruction: the global viewpoint]{.tag} The *Crust* of Amenta–Bern (1999) proves: a sufficiently fine $\varepsilon$-sample of the surface $S$ + Voronoi/Delaunay = a reconstruction homeomorphic to $S$ (topological guarantee); the *Poisson surface reconstruction* (Kazhdan et al., 2006) changes paradigm: fit an "inside/outside" indicator function $\chi$ whose gradient matches the oriented normals $\nabla\chi \approx \mathbf{n}\,\delta_S$ — a Poisson problem $\Delta \chi = \nabla \cdot (\mathbf{n}\,\delta_S)$ solved in multi-resolution; robust to holes and non-uniform data. Recent approaches learn SDFs (deep learning on meshes — cf. Multimodal GenAI module, 3D chapter), but the evaluation is always done by marching cubes: the tool has not aged a bit.
:::

::: def
[Definition 4.6 — Rigid registration: the ICP algorithm]{.tag} Before reconstructing, one often has to *align* several acquisitions of the same object: this is **rigid registration** — seeking $R \in SO(3)$ and $t$ applied to the cloud $P$ to fit it onto $Q$. The **ICP** algorithm (*iterative closest point*, Besl–McKay, 1992) alternates:

1.  **match**: each point of $P$ to its nearest neighbor in $Q$ (kd-tree);
2.  **align**: the optimal rigid transform in the least-squares sense on these pairs is solved exactly by singular value decomposition of the cross-covariance matrix (the Kabsch–Umeyama solution, implemented by the Computer Vision module);
3.  **iterate** until the residual converges.

Each step can only decrease the error, so the algorithm converges — but to a *local minimum*: initialization matters (crude or geodesic transform), and robust variants reject outlier pairs (quantile distance), weight by normals or minimize the point-to-plane error. It is the universal tool of 3D scanning and cloud fusion — rigid only: non-rigid correspondence waits for chapter 8.
:::

## 5. Smoothing: from uniform to cotangent Laplacian {#ch5}

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — Combinatorial Laplacian and smoothing scheme]{.tag} On a closed mesh, the **uniform (combinatorial) Laplacian** of a vertex $i$ with neighborhood $\mathcal{N}(i)$ is $\delta_i = \dfrac{1}{\|\mathcal{N}(i)\|}\sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}(i)} p_j - p_i$, and **Laplacian smoothing** iterates $$p_i \leftarrow p_i + \lambda\,\delta_i, \qquad \lambda \in (0, 1].$$ This is a *local projection* method; "mean curvature flow" version: $p_i \leftarrow p_i + \lambda\,H_i \mathbf{n}_i$ (chapter 7 for $H_i$). In matrix form: $\mathbf{x} \leftarrow (I - \lambda L)\,\mathbf{x}$ with $L = D^{-1}A - I$ (normalized) or $L = D - A$ (non-normalized).
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.2 — Uniform smoothing shrinks: 1D spectral proof]{.tag} On a ring of $n$ vertices (cycle) with positions $x_i$, the iteration $x_i \leftarrow (1-\lambda)x_i + \lambda \bar{x}_{\mathcal{N}(i)}$ preserves the mean $\bar{x}$ and makes every non-constant component decrease: $x^{(k)} \to \bar{x}\mathbf{1}$ — the 1D mesh *shrinks* down to the barycenter. The decay rate of a mode of frequency $j$ is $\rho_j = 1 - \lambda\big(1 - \cos\tfrac{2\pi j}{n}\big) \in [0, 1)$.

::: proof
Decompose $x$ on the orthogonal basis of discrete Fourier modes $u^{(j)}_i = e^{2i\pi ji/n}$. The average of neighbors multiplies $u^{(j)}$ by $\frac{1}{2}(e^{2i\pi j/n} + e^{-2i\pi j/n}) = \cos\frac{2\pi j}{n}$; hence the iteration multiplies mode $j$ by $(1-\lambda) + \lambda\cos\frac{2\pi j}{n}$. For $j = 0$ (constant): factor 1 — conservation of the mean. For $j \neq 0$: $\cos\frac{2\pi j}{n} < 1$ gives $\rho_j < 1$ (and $\geq -1$ for $\lambda \leq 1$): all non-constant modes decay geometrically, high frequencies fastest. Limit = constant component = barycenter. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 5.3 — Remedies: Taubin λ\|μ, cotangents]{.tag}

-   **Taubin λ\|μ**: alternate a smoothing step ($\lambda \approx 0.5$) and an "unsmoothing" step ($\mu \approx -0.53$); the frequencies in the pass band $(\rho_\mu, \rho_\lambda)$ are preserved — the mean volume is conserved instead of collapsing;
-   **Cotangent (geometric) Laplacian**: $$\delta_i = \frac{1}{2 A_i}\sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}(i)} \big(\cot \alpha_{ij} + \cot \beta_{ij}\big)\,(p_j - p_i),$$ where $\alpha_{ij}, \beta_{ij}$ are the angles opposite the edge $(i,j)$ and $A_i$ the mixed Voronoi area of the vertex — this is the operator converging to the Laplace–Beltrami operator (theory of hat function forms; cf. Geometric Deep Learning module, operators chapter);
-   **Filtering order**: smoothing in *position* regularizes geometry; smoothing the *normals* then re-projecting (or shrink-and-grow) separates denoising from deformation — the two families coexist in DCCs.
:::

::: ex
[Example 5.4 — Cotangents on an isosceles right triangle]{.tag} Single triangle $A = (0,0)$, $B = (1,0)$, $C = (0,1)$, vertex $A$. Its two adjacent edges are $(A,B)$ and $(A,C)$: for edge $(A,B)$, the opposite angle is $\angle ACB = 90°$, of zero cotangent; for edge $(A,C)$, the opposite $\angle ABC = 90°$, zero cotangent as well. Edge $(B,C)$ is not adjacent to $A$: the sum of cotangents around $A$ is zero, $\delta_A = 0$ — consistent, a mesh reduced to a single triangle is "all boundary". The real implementation test is the *planar test*: embed a planar mesh in its plane ⟹ all interior $\delta_i$ are zero (discrete equivalent of $\Delta f = 0$ for harmonic functions). The proof comes from the discrete Green formula: $\sum_i A_i\, f_i\, \delta_i = -\sum_{(i,j)} w_{ij}(f_j - f_i)^2 \leq 0$, with equality if and only if $f$ is constant on each component.
:::

::: note
[From smoothing to geometric deep learning]{.tag} The cotangent matrix *is* the central object of the M2 Geometric Deep Learning module: diffusion of descriptors (HKS), spectral convolutions (eigenfunction bases, chapter 8 below), DiffusionNet. The smoothing of this chapter is its "deterministic" version: same operator, without learned data — and already non-trivial: choice of area/mixed Voronoi, negative weights on obtuse meshes (to be truncated or regularized).
:::

## 6. Simplification and remeshing {#ch6}

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — Quadric Error Metrics (QEM)]{.tag} To each vertex $v$ one associates the set $\mathcal{P}(v)$ of the planes of its supported faces; its **error quadric** is $$E(v) = \sum_{\pi \in \mathcal{P}(v)} \big(\mathbf{n}_\pi \cdot v - d_\pi\big)^2 = v^\top\!A v + 2\,b^\top v + c, \qquad A = \sum_{\pi} \mathbf{n}_\pi \mathbf{n}_\pi^\top,\ \ b = -\sum_\pi d_\pi \mathbf{n}_\pi,\ \ c = \sum_\pi d_\pi^2.$$ **Edge contraction** $(u, v) \to \bar{v}$: choose $\bar{v}$ minimizing $E_{u \oplus v}$ (the sum quadric), then merge. The order of contractions follows increasing cost (priority queue): this is the Garland–Heckbert algorithm (1997), still the standard for game LODs.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.2 — Additivity of quadrics and algebraic optimum]{.tag} (i) $E_{u \oplus v}(x) = E_u(x) + E_v(x)$ for every $x$ — the quadrics add coefficient by coefficient $(A, b, c) = (A_u + A_v,\ b_u + b_v,\ c_u + c_v)$. (ii) If $A = A_u + A_v$ is invertible, the minimal cost of the contraction is attained at $\bar{v} = -A^{-1}b$ and equals $c - b^\top A^{-1} b$.

::: proof
\(i\) Each quadric is a *sum* of squares over sets of planes; merging the vertices merges the sets of planes (the incident faces become incident to the merged vertex), and the sum of sums is the sum over the union — hence the term-by-term additivity of the quadratic forms. (ii) $E(x) = x^\top A x + 2b^\top x + c$, $A$ symmetric positive definite: $\nabla E = 2(Ax + b) = 0$ gives $x^\ast = -A^{-1}b$, and $E(x^\ast) = c - b^\top A^{-1}b$ (direct substitution). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 6.3 — Two contractions with numbers]{.tag}

-   **1D straight boundary**: two vertices of a straight edge carry the planes $x = 0$ and $x = 2$ (unit normal $(1,0,0)$, offsets 0 and 2); $E(x) = x^2 + (x-2)^2 = 2(x-1)^2 + 2$, minimal at $\bar{v} = (1,0,0)$ at cost 2 — the contraction "glues" the two planes halfway;
-   **Cube corner**: planes $x=0, y=0, z=0$ (unit normals). $A = I_3$, $b = 0$, $c = 0$ ⟹ $\bar{v} = (0,0,0)$, cost 0: contracting the three faces of a cube corner toward the exact corner costs *nothing* — this is the strength of QEM: detecting exact algebraic folds.
:::

::: def
[Definition 6.4 — Isotropic remeshing]{.tag} Transforming a mesh into a quasi-uniform mesh (edge lengths in $[l_{\min}, l_{\max}]$, roughly equilateral triangles) by the loop: (1) **split** of overly long edges (projected midpoint); (2) **collapse** of overly short ones; (3) edge **flip** restoring valence 6 (interior) / 4 (boundary); (4) tangential smoothing (chapter 5, projected onto the tangent plane so as not to shrink the shape). Result: a mesh suited to the simulations of the Computer Animation module and to the convolutions of the Geometric Deep Learning module. **Parameterization** (chart atlas) is the alternative: cut into topological disks, flatten (Tutte/harmonic, ARAP), remesh *in the parameter domain* — higher quality, more delicate handling of cuts.
:::

::: note
[Errors on a budget]{.tag} In production, simplification is both *judge and jury*: the QEM quadric optimizes an algebraic error (distance to planes), not the Hausdorff distance to the original surface — boundaries and fine details require *locks* (preserved edges/attributes) and weighted boundary planes; for attributes (color, normals), one stacks quadrics of "planes" in higher dimension. Rule of thumb: a 10:1 reduction ratio is almost invisible on screen on dense meshes — beyond that, steer by curvature fields (chapter 7) to decide *where* to keep the triangles.
:::

::: def
[Definition 6.5 — Surface subdivision]{.tag} Subdivision is the reverse path of simplification: start from a coarse *control mesh* and refine it iteratively by local rules, up to a smooth *limit* surface. The **Loop** scheme (1987, triangular) cuts each triangle into four through the edge midpoints: each *new* edge vertex takes $\tfrac38(v_i + v_j) + \tfrac18(v_a + v_b)$ (endpoints and the two opposite neighbors), each *old* vertex slides toward $(1 - n\beta)\,v + \beta\sum_{\text{neighbors}} v_i$ with $\beta$ depending on the valence $n$. In the limit, the surface is a quartic B-spline $C^2$ everywhere, except at **extraordinary vertices** (valence $\neq 6$) where it remains $C^1$. The **Catmull–Clark** scheme (1978) is its quadrilateral analogue (bicubic B-spline; extraordinary vertices of valence $\neq 4$) — the standard of animated film, which the Computer Animation module meets on the rendering side. Theory: these rules extend to surfaces the de Casteljau refinement of curves (def. 1.6); subdivision and simplification thus bracket the level of detail of a single shape, from the control mesh to the rendering mesh.
:::

## 7. Discrete curvature and Gauss–Bonnet {#ch7}

::: def
[Definition 7.1 — Curvatures in the continuous setting, to set the targets]{.tag} At a point of a smooth surface, the principal directions have extreme normal curvatures $\kappa_1, \kappa_2$; **Gaussian curvature** $K = \kappa_1 \kappa_2$ (product); **mean curvature** $H = \tfrac{\kappa_1 + \kappa_2}{2}$ (average); the shape operator satisfies $H = \tfrac12 \mathrm{div}\, \mathbf{n}$ — hence the link with the Laplacian of chapter 5: $\Delta x = -2H\mathbf{n}$. $K$ is intrinsic (measurable "from within the surface"); $H$ depends on the embedding — this distinction structures all of shape analysis.
:::

::: def
[Definition 7.2 — Angle deficit]{.tag} At vertex $i$ of a triangulated mesh, the **angle deficit** is $$\mathcal{K}_i = 2\pi - \sum_{j}\,\theta_{ij},$$ the sum of the angles of the faces incident at $i$. It is the natural discretization of the Gaussian curvature *integrated* over the neighborhood: positive at tips (cone), zero on developable zones, negative at passes (saddle). The **discrete mean curvature** is obtained by the discrete Steiner theorem: $\mathbf{H}_i = \frac{1}{2 A_i} \sum_j (\cot\alpha_{ij} + \cot\beta_{ij})(p_j - p_i)$ — the same cotangent matrix as in chapter 5: geometry and analysis are one.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 7.3 — Discrete Gauss–Bonnet]{.tag} For a closed mesh of genus $g$: $$\sum_{i \in V} \mathcal{K}_i = 2\pi\,\chi = 2\pi\,(2 - 2g),$$ where $\chi = V - E + F$ is the Euler characteristic (chapter 9). The total curvature depends only on the topology — not on the geometry.

::: proof
*Counting.* The double sum of angles runs over all the angles of all the faces: each triangle contributes $\pi$, so $\sum_i \sum_j \theta_{ij} = \pi F$ and $\sum_i \mathcal{K}_i = 2\pi V - \pi F$. Each face has 3 edges and each edge carries 2 faces: $3F = 2E$, so $2\pi E = 3\pi F$, hence $$-2\pi E + 2\pi F = -3\pi F + 2\pi F = -\pi F \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 2\pi(V - E + F) = 2\pi V - \pi F = \sum_i \mathcal{K}_i.$$ *Verification on the cube* (Example 7.4 below): $8$ vertices of deficit $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ give $4\pi = 2\pi \cdot 2$, consistent with $\chi = V - E + F = 8 - 12 + 6 = 2$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 7.4 — Regular tetrahedron, and subdivisions]{.tag} Regular tetrahedron: each vertex carries 3 angles of 60° ⟹ $\mathcal{K} = 2\pi - \pi = \pi$, total $4\pi$ = that of the cube — same topological sphere, very different local curvatures ("pointy" vertices of the tetrahedron), same *total*. Subdividing each face of the cube into 4 triangles (mid-edges): the new edge vertices are flat (zero deficit: $2\pi$ of angles around them), the 8 corners keep the same deficit $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ — the sum is unchanged: the theorem is *invariant under subdivision*, an indispensable condition for "discrete curvature" to converge to the continuous curvature as the mesh is refined.
:::

::: note
[Estimating in practice]{.tag} Deficits give an *integrated* curvature; for a *pointwise* curvature, divide by the mixed Voronoi area $A_i$: $K_i \approx \mathcal{K}_i / A_i$, with the same areas as in chapter 5. For noisy meshes, smooth first (chapter 5) — curvature is a *second derivative*, twice as sensitive to noise as positions. These descriptors ($K_i, H_i$, principal directions) directly feed: adaptive remeshing (chapter 6), the descriptors of Geometric Deep Learning, and direction fields for quadrangulation.
:::

## 8. The spectrum of shapes {#ch8}

::: def
[Definition 8.1 — Laplace–Beltrami and spectrum]{.tag} On a compact boundaryless surface $S$, the **Laplace–Beltrami** operator $\Delta_S$ (surface Laplacian) is self-adjoint, negative, with compact resolvent: its spectrum is a sequence $$0 = \lambda_0 < \lambda_1 \leq \lambda_2 \leq \dots \to \infty,$$ with orthonormal eigenfunctions $\phi_0, \phi_1, \dots$ (a basis of $L^2(S)$). The **spectrum** $\{\lambda_k\}$ (or its sampling $(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_N)$, "ShapeDNA") is an *isometric invariant*: two isometric surfaces have the same spectrum. In practice: discretize by the generalized cotangent matrix $L = A^{-1}W$ (chapter 5) and solve the *generalized eigenvalue problem* $W\phi = \lambda A \phi$, with $A$ the diagonal matrix of mixed Voronoi areas — the same objects as in chapters 5 and 7.
:::

::: ex
[Example 8.2 — Exact spectra: path graph and cycle]{.tag} For the combinatorial Laplacian of a path with $n$ vertices (chain): $$\lambda_k = 2 - 2\cos\frac{k\pi}{n+1}, \qquad k = 1, \dots, n,$$ and for the cycle with $n$ vertices (closed ring): $\mu_k = 2 - 2\cos\frac{2\pi k}{n}$. For $n = 10$ path: $\lambda_1 = 2 - 2\cos(\pi/11) \approx 0.081$, $\lambda_{10} \approx 3.919$; cycle: $\mu_1 \approx 0.382$, $\mu_5 = 4$ (alternation ±1, the highest possible frequency). Geometric reading: closing the chain "tightens" the lowest frequency ($\lambda_1$ multiplied by \~4.7): the smallest eigenvalue measures the *connectedness / tightness* of the shape — it is what discriminates components and pinch points (the applications of spectral segmentation).
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 8.3 — Heat kernel and spectral signatures]{.tag} The solution of the heat equation $\partial_t u = -\Delta_S u$, $u(0) = f$, writes $u(t) = e^{-t\Delta_S}f = \sum_k e^{-\lambda_k t} \langle f, \phi_k\rangle \phi_k$ and the **heat kernel** $h_t(x, y) = \sum_k e^{-\lambda_k t}\phi_k(x)\phi_k(y)$ is an isometric invariant. Pointwise signatures (HKS: $h_t(x, x)$ for a few $t$; WKS: oscillation) describe each point by "its" place in the spectrum — the basis of non-rigid shape correspondence, detailed in the M2 Geometric Deep Learning module (signatures chapter). The converse "spectrum ⟹ shape" is false: there exist *isospectral non-isometric* surfaces ("you cannot hear the shape of a drum", Gordon–Webb–Wolpert, 1992).
:::

::: note
[Interpretations and uses]{.tag} The eigenvalue $\lambda_k$ is the square of a spatial frequency: small $k$ = large undulations (silhouette), large $k$ = details. Direct applications: shape compression (projecting onto the $\phi_k$ of small $k$), correspondence (coordination of eigenbases), retrieval (vector $(\sqrt{\lambda_1}, \dots, \sqrt{\lambda_N})$ renormalized by scale), segmentation (cutting along the level lines of $\phi_2$, the "Fiedler function"). Numerical caution: only the first \~$\sqrt{N}$ eigenvalues of a discretization with $N$ vertices are reliable — beyond that, one describes the mesh, not the surface (same phenomenon as numerical dispersion in finite elements).
:::

::: def
[Definition 8.4 — Shape recognition, non-rigid matching and correspondence]{.tag} **Recognition**: measuring the *similarity* of two shapes $S, T$. The spectral signatures ("ShapeDNA" spectrum of definition 8.1, heat kernel of proposition 8.3) give fast retrieval; the **Gromov–Hausdorff** distance — comparing the intrinsic *geodesic distance matrices* — compares without a common embedding. **Non-rigid matching**: the two shapes are two poses of a single articulated object (a sitting or standing character) — related by a *quasi-isometry* $T$ that preserves geodesic distances up to a factor $\varepsilon$; the intrinsic descriptors (HKS, WKS) are then stable and match point to point. **Correspondence**: the map $x \mapsto T(x)$ itself. The *functional maps* approach (Ovsjanikov et al., 2012) represents it by the transport operator of functions on the surface, which becomes *diagonal* in the eigenbases of the two Laplacians: a small $k \times k$ matrix to estimate — constrained by the HKS/WKS pairs and the preservation of signals — before conversion into a point-to-point map. It is the official entry gate of the "non-rigid matching and correspondence" of the syllabus, extended in M2 by Analysis and Deep Learning on Geometric Data.
:::

## 9. Combinatorial topology: Euler, Betti, persistence {#ch9}

::: thm
[Theorem 9.1 — Euler–Poincaré formula]{.tag} For every connected closed mesh of genus $g$: $$\chi = V - E + F = 2 - 2g,$$ and more generally for an arbitrary complex $\chi = \sum_{k} (-1)^k c_k$ ($c_k$ = number of cells of dimension $k$) $= \sum_k (-1)^k b_k$ (Betti numbers). *Proof sketch* for a sphere: start from the tetrahedron ($\chi = 2$, Example 1.4) and note that subdividing a face (adding a vertex on an edge or at the center of a face) does not change $\chi$ (an edge split: $+1$ vertex, $+1$ edge; a face split: $+1$ vertex, $+3$ edges, $+2$ faces — $\Delta\chi = 0$ in both cases); any triangulation of the sphere is obtained from the tetrahedron by these operations. Adding a "handle" subtracts 2 from $\chi$ — hence $2 - 2g$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: def
[Definition 9.2 — Homology and Betti numbers]{.tag} On a complex $K$, the homology groups $H_k(K)$ (with coefficients in $\mathbb{Z}_2$, to simplify) are the classes of cycles modulo boundaries: $H_k = \ker \partial_k / \mathrm{im}\, \partial_{k+1}$, with $\partial_k \partial_{k+1} = 0$ (the boundary of a boundary is zero). The **Betti numbers** $b_k = \dim H_k$ count the independent "holes": for a closed surface: $b_0$ connected components, $b_1$ = $2g$ handles, $b_2$ = 1 if orientable (the volume itself). Examples: sphere $(1, 0, 1)$, torus $(1, 2, 1)$, double torus $(1, 4, 1)$; check: $\chi = b_0 - b_1 + b_2$ ✓. Homology is computed by Gaussian elimination on the boundary matrices (Smith normal form): purely combinatorial algorithms, polynomial cost.
:::

::: def
[Definition 9.3 — Persistent homology]{.tag} Let a **filtration** $K_0 \subseteq K_1 \subseteq \dots \subseteq K_m$ (e.g.: alpha-shapes $(\mathcal{C}_\alpha)_\alpha$ of chapter 4, or sublevel sets of a function on the mesh). At each step, cycles are born and die; the **persistence** of a cycle is $\mathrm{pers} = \alpha_{death} - \alpha_{birth}$. The **diagram/barcode** (one bar $[\alpha_{birth}, \alpha_{death}]$ per class) separates structure (long bars) from noise (short bars); the stability theorem guarantees that the barcode changes little when the data change little — this is what makes TDA usable on real data. Standard implementation: column reduction algorithm (boundary matrix of the filtration, Gaussian pivot), in $O(m^\omega)$ worst case, quasi-linear in practice.
:::

::: ex
[Example 9.4 — A noisy ring, read by persistence]{.tag} 1,000 points sampling a ring (disk of radius 2 with a hole of radius 1) + Gaussian noise σ = 0.1. Filtration by alpha-shapes: $H_0$ bars: 999 short ones (merging clusters, all $\alpha \lesssim 0.2$) + 1 infinite (the component); $H_1$ bars: one long bar $[0.25\,;\,2.0]$ — the central hole — plus a few bars of length $< 0.2$ (small noise holes plugged early). With σ = 0.4, the central bar survives $[0.4\,;\,1.7]$: persistence, unlike counting at fixed $\alpha$, is *robust to noise*. It is the most widely used topological descriptor for learning (vectorizations of persistence diagrams, persistence kernels — cf. the team's work, chapter 10).
:::

::: note
[Topology and learning]{.tag} The invariants of this chapter serve as *structural regularizers* in learning: persistence loss to reconstruct with the right number of components/holes, genus constraints in mesh generation (the Multimodal GenAI module, 3D chapter, returns to this); the Gauss–Bonnet theorem (chapter 7) is the "curvature" case of the same idea: global quantities that constrain local solutions.
:::

## 10. Course research notes (Desbrun, Memari) {#ch10}

::: def
[Mathieu Desbrun — discrete differential geometry]{.tag} M. Desbrun (Caltech / Inria associate) is one of the founders of discrete exterior calculus and of the discrete geometric operators that structure this module:

-   **Discrete Exterior Calculus** (with A. Hirani, M. Leok, J. Marsden, 2005) — [arXiv math/0508341](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0508341): a theory of differential forms on simplicial complexes that preserves the identities of the continuum *exactly* (Stokes, Hodge): the cotangent Laplacians of chapter 5 and the curvatures of chapter 7 are instances of it;
-   **Discrete Differential Forms for Computational Modeling** (with E. Kanso, Y. Tong) — [Springer chapter](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-7643-8621-4_16): the pedagogical version (why the "naive" discretization of operators loses the structure);
-   The course **Digital Geometry Processing with Discrete Exterior Calculus** (K. Crane, F. de Goes, M. Desbrun, P. Schröder, SIGGRAPH Asia 2013) — [ACM DL](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2504435.2504442) / [open DDG notes](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~kmcrane/Projects/DDG/): the reference for the labs (libigl), from the Laplacian to geometric flows.
:::

::: def
[Pooran Memari — topology and reconstruction of shapes]{.tag} CNRS senior researcher at LIX (École Polytechnique), P. Memari works at the interface of algorithmic geometry / topology:

-   **Geometric Tomography with Topological Guarantees** (with O. Amini, J.-D. Boissonnat, Discrete & Computational Geometry, 2013) — [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/1007.2452) / [Springer](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00454-013-9531-z): reconstructing a 3D solid from 2D cross-sections (serial microscopy); the analysis shows why naive reconstructions fail (two solids of different topologies can have the *same* cross-sections) and gives guarantees — exactly the "sample, reconstruct, guarantee" program of chapter 4;
-   Her HDR thesis, **"Points, Patterns and Shapes: towards accessible geometric modeling"** (2024), synthesizes this program: point patterns (sampling, chapter 4), proximity structures (Voronoi/Delaunay, chapters 2–3), accessibility of modeling tools — page: [LIX](https://www.lix.polytechnique.fr/~memari/);
-   Her work on *distributed* Delaunay triangulations (Tile & Merge, IEEE Big Data 2019) extends chapter 3 to cloud scale: meshing billions of points by cutting space into tiles whose Delaunay triangulations stitch back together.
:::

::: note
[Common thread]{.tag} The two research programs meet on one principle: *a discretization must preserve the structure* — differential identities on one side (Desbrun: exact discrete Stokes), topological invariants on the other (Memari: homeomorphism-type guarantees). This is the ridge line of the whole module: represent *faithfully* before analyzing, then learn — the gateway to Geometric Deep Learning (M2).
:::

## Exercises {#ex}

1.  **Guided duality.** For the sites $p_1 = (0,0)$, $p_2 = (4,0)$, $p_3 = (0,3)$ of Example 2.4: (a) verify that $(2, 1.5)$ is at distance 2.5 from the three sites; (b) draw the three perpendicular bisectors and the unbounded cell of $p_2$; (c) add $p_4 = (4,3)$ — why are the four points cocircular, and which Delaunay triangulations does one obtain (lift the degeneracy by perturbation)?
2.  **Empty circle criterion.** In a convex quadrilateral, $\angle abc = 70°$ and $\angle adc = 125°$ (diagonal $ac$). (a) Decide whether a flip is needed (Lemma 3.2). (b) After the flip, what is at least the smallest of the angles opposite the new diagonal? (c) Prove point (ii) of the proof: $b \in \mathrm{disk}(a,c,d) \iff d \in \mathrm{disk}(a,b,c)$ for a convex quadrilateral.
3.  **Guided lift and incircle.** (a) Implement the test of Theorem 3.4: for each triangle of `Delaunay` (scipy), construct the plane $\Pi$ and verify that no lifted point is under $\Pi$ (tolerance $10^{-12}$). (b) Compare with the incircle determinant (signs: interior/exterior). (c) Perturb a point toward the circumcircle of a neighboring triangle: observe the flip in the computed triangulation.
4.  **Lloyd.** (a) Show that Lloyd relaxation decreases the quantization energy $\mathcal{E} = \sum_i \int_{\mathcal{V}(p_i)} \|x - p_i\|^2\,dx$ (each iteration is an alternation: optimal cells for the sites, then optimal centroids for the cells). (b) Implement and plot $\mathcal{E}$ (approximated by sampling) as a function of iterations on 100 points of the square.
5.  **Guided shrinking.** (a) Complete the proof of Theorem 5.2: why does mode $j$ decay exactly like $\rho_j^k$? What happens for $\lambda > 1$? (b) Simulate a ring of radius 1, $n = 50$, $\lambda = 0.5$; plot the mean radius — by how much does it shrink in 100 iterations? (c) Apply Taubin $\lambda = 0.5$, $\mu = -0.53$ and measure.
6.  **QEM.** (a) Recover Example 6.3 (cube corner) in detail: write $A, b, c$, verify $A = I$. (b) Two perpendicular planes $x = 0, y = 0$ plus a "ceiling" plane $z = 1$: where does the optimal point fall and what is the cost? (c) Implement quadric edge contractions on a torus mesh (libigl) and plot the Hausdorff error as a function of the number of faces.
7.  **Gauss–Bonnet.** (a) Verify Theorem 7.3 on the tetrahedron and the cube (by hand), then on the minimal $3 \times 3$ torus (9 vertices, 27 edges, 18 faces — $\chi = 0$). (b) Show that an edge split does not change $\chi$ (counting). (c) Subdivide the cube 3 times and numerically verify the invariance of the total deficit.
8.  **Spectra.** (a) Prove the formula of Example 8.2 for the path (verify that $u^{(k)}_i = \sin\frac{k\pi i}{n+1}$ is an eigenvector). (b) Compute the first 10 cotangent eigenvalues of a flat strip mesh and of the same bent strip (isometric); compare. (c) Discuss: why do the spectra diverge in practice (sampling, triangulation) while theory predicts equality?
9.  **Guided persistence.** (a) Build the alpha-shapes filtration of a noisy ring (exercise of chapter 9); extract the $H_1$ barcode (gudhi or ripser). (b) Increase the noise until the long bar disappears: at what σ does this happen, and why is the prediction "σ ≈ hole radius / 3" reasonable? (c) Replace the ring by two rings and verify $b_1 = 2$.
